analysis.one_liner: Authorizes the annual Defense Department budget: weapons and war funding, plus military pay, health benefits, and sexual assault protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 341-48, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and the President signed it into law on January 7, 2011 as Public Law 111-383.
analysis.plain_summary: This is the annual bill that sets the Defense Department's legal budget for fiscal year 2011. It authorizes money for weapons, ships, aircraft, and operations in Afghanistan and Iraq, and it sets troop levels. It also carries things that touch service members and their families directly: a one-year freeze on TRICARE premiums and pharmacy copays, coverage for children up to age 26, new sexual assault prevention offices and victim advocates, and payments to Guam residents who suffered under the World War II Japanese occupation. It restricts the use of federal money to move Guantanamo detainees to the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members and military families get the most tangible provisions: TRICARE premiums, inpatient charges, and pharmacy copays are frozen for a year, dependent children can stay on TRICARE until 26, family caregivers get stipends matched to the VA program, disability review boards become available to enlisted members, and sexual assault victims are entitled to advocates. Guam World War II survivors and their families get authorized claims payments. Defense contractors receive authorized funding for aircraft, ships, missiles, ammunition, and war operations, and the bill requires the Navy to keep maintaining and upgrading certain intelligence aircraft rather than retiring them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members, military families, and defense contractors

how_it_helps.text: Freezes TRICARE Prime premiums, TRICARE Standard inpatient charges and reserve premiums, and caps retail pharmacy copays at $3 generic, $9 formulary, and $22 nonformulary for the year [S4].
Lets TRICARE beneficiaries keep dependent children covered up to age 26 if they are not eligible for an employer plan, effective January 1, 2011 [S4].
Establishes a Director of the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response Office, entitles victims to a Sexual Assault Victim Advocate, and requires annual reports on sexual assaults through 2017 [S4].
Directs Treasury to pay claims to living Guam residents who were raped, injured, interned, or subjected to forced labor during the World War II occupation, with payments to survivors afterward [S4].
Matches the DOD family caregiver stipend to the VA comprehensive caregiver program and extends disability review boards to enlisted members [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the authorized Defense Department and Department of Energy national security budgets, including procurement of aircraft, ships, and munitions and continued funding for operations in Afghanistan and Iraq [S4]. The bill also locks in restrictions on transferring or releasing Guantanamo detainees using federal funds, keeping the detention facility's population in place, and it repeals conditions that had limited expansion of contractor-performed depot maintenance while barring quotas for converting contractor work to federal employees [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers funding weapons, war operations, and contractor roles

drawbacks.text: Blocks the use of any funds in the Act to transfer or release Guantanamo detainees to the United States and requires 30-day congressional certification before transfers to foreign countries, constraining the administration's stated goal of closing the facility [S4].

Repeals conditions on expanding prime vendor contracts for depot-level maintenance and bars the Defense Secretary from setting goals or quotas for converting contractor functions to civilian DOD employees, preserving the contractor role in work that had been targeted for insourcing [S4].

Authorizes tens of billions of dollars in procurement — including $18.9 billion in Navy aircraft and $15.7 billion in shipbuilding — while relying mainly on reports and management plans rather than structural cost controls for programs like the F-35 [S4].
Delays until January 1, 2015 a legal deadline to reduce the number of deputy under secretaries of defense and allows up to five additional deputy under secretaries in the meantime [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit provisions for military families are real and immediate: a year of frozen TRICARE costs, expanded dependent coverage, caregiver stipend parity, and sexual assault response improvements. The costs are the other side of the same coin: the bill authorizes the full annual defense budget — including war operations and large weapons procurement — and in several places protects the contractor status quo, from depot maintenance to private security firms, rather than shrinking it. The Guantanamo provisions remove the administration's funding path for moving detainees onto US soil. Readers should weigh the service-member benefits against the fact that this is the vehicle that keeps the entire defense budget and its contractor relationships running for another year.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 341-48 under a fast-track procedure requiring two-thirds support, the Senate amended and passed it by unanimous consent two days before Christmas, the House agreed to the Senate's changes without objection, and the President signed it on January 7, 2011 [S8][S9].

narrative.text: Introduced December 15, 2010 and referred to the Armed Services and Budget Committees; no cosponsors [S1][S7].
On December 17 the House passed it under suspension of the rules, a procedure that allows a bill to move quickly but requires a two-thirds vote and allows no amendments, 341-48 [S8][S9].
The Senate passed it with an amendment by unanimous consent on December 22, 2010 [S8].
The House agreed to the Senate amendments by unanimous consent the same day, and the bill was signed by the President on January 7, 2011, becoming Public Law 111-383 [S8][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors come out ahead with another year of authorized procurement and war funding, and the contractor role in depot maintenance and war-zone security is preserved. Military families also gain from the TRICARE freezes and benefit expansions, while the Guantanamo transfer restrictions mean the detention population largely stays put.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was 341-48 with 187 of 253 Democrats and 154 of 178 Republicans in favor, and the Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent with no recorded opposition [S9][S8].

industries.note: The bill authorizes tens of billions for aircraft, ships, missiles, and ammunition, and requires the Navy to keep maintaining rather than retire certain intelligence aircraft, keeping contracts flowing [S4]. It also adds oversight of contractor business systems and cost estimating, but leaves the industry as the permanent channel for weapons and war support [S4].

The bill extends DOD regulation of contractors performing private security functions to new regions including Yemen, the Horn of Africa, and the Philippines, and tightens accountability remedies, while continuing their role in war zones [S4].

The bill requires that small arms ammunition exceeding military needs be sold commercially rather than destroyed, with first offer to law enforcement and other agencies, putting surplus military ammunition on the civilian market [S4].
The bill extends the Maritime Security Fleet program authorization through fiscal year 2025 and funds the Maritime Administration, continuing federal support for a US-flag merchant fleet [S4].
